item.title: AEW star Adam Copeland reflects on opportunity to compete at iconic Mexican venue
item.description: Adam Copeland calls Arena México 'The Wrestling Cathedral' as he prepares for his first match in Mexico since 2008 at AEW Grand Slam: Mexico.
item.content:encoded:
It’s hard to believe someone as legendary as Adam Copeland has never competed in an iconic venue like Arena México, but on Wednesday night he will get his first opportunity.

Copeland will be a part of an eight-man tag team match at All Elite Wrestling’s (AEW) Grand Slam: Mexico event on Wednesday night. Copeland and his tag team partner Christian Cage (AEW’s tag team champions) will team with Matt and Nick Jackson to take on Jon Moxley, Daniel Garcia, Pac and Wheeler Yuta.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON FOX NEWS DIGITAL

Copeland reflected on the chance to compete at the iconic Mexico City venue in a post on Instagram.

"Tonight I get to perform for the first time in The Wrestling Cathedral," he wrote in the post. "Arena Mexico. The last time I had a match in Mexico was 2008. Mexico we got some catching up to do! I love Lucha Libre. Everything about it. The masks, the mystique, the pageantry. Can’t wait to get out there. See ya soon Mexico, bring your voices."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Copeland previously wrote down a list of venues he wanted to perform in. Arena México was at the top of the list along with Wembley Stadium in London, Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto and the Tokyo Dome in Japan.

He will likely get to check off Wembley Stadium from his list when AEW holds its premier pay-per-view of the year, All In, at the venue later this month.

Copeland and Cage won the AEW World Tag Team Championship at Double or Nothing in a brutal I Quit match against FTR. They’ve held the titles ever since and appear to be the ones walking into Wembley Stadium as the champions if they have any formidable challengers.

item.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Medicare-for-all crusade collides with an awkward contradiction involving his wife
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed pushes Medicare for All, but his wife's psychiatry practice refuses all insurance, forcing patients to pay entirely out of pocket.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has campaigned on passing Medicare-for-all, but his wife’s private psychiatry practice appears to operate outside the insurance system entirely.

El-Sayed, who secured the Democratic nomination for Senate on Wednesday, has argued that "healthcare shouldn't depend on who signs your paycheck" and demanded that taxpayers pay to "guarantee healthcare from cradle to grave" through Medicare-for-all. Despite this, his wife, Sarah Jukaku, states on her medical practice’s website that she is out of network with all insurance companies, generally requiring patients to pay the practice directly, though some may be eligible for out-of-network reimbursement.

Prior to July 2026, the FAQ section of Jukaku's website for her practice included the question "do you accept my insurance?" accompanied by the answer "no," according to the Washington Free Beacon. Her profile on Psychology Today, a popular professional database for therapists and psychiatrists, also at one point noted that she did not accept insurance.

Jukaku operates her own practice where she is the sole physician.

Amid media scrutiny in July, the practice’s website became inaccessible to the public and displayed a message indicating that it was private. Fox News Digital reached Jukaku and her practice multiple times via phone and email but received no response.

DR MARC SIEGEL: A SENATE CANDIDATE'S MEDICAL TITLE SPARKS A DEBATE VOTERS SHOULDN'T IGNORE

It is not rare for psychiatrists to turn away patients on Medicare. A 2022 analysis by KFF found that 40% of psychiatrists did not participate in Medicare, among the highest rate of any medical specialty.

Even as his wife's psychiatry practice reportedly operates on an out-of-network model, El-Sayed has repeatedly stressed the importance of expanding access to government-backed healthcare.

In a 2020 interview with the National Alliance on Mental Illness, for instance, he stated that "my wife's a psychiatrist, and we talk about the fact that a lot of folks don't do psychiatry because it's not as well recompensed as other practices simply because it's undervalued in the system." He went on to argue that the United States needs to build a "system" that "recognizes" the importance of treating "mental illness" due to the prevalence of "serious mental illness" and "death by suicide."

Years later, at a September 2025 campaign event, El-Sayed lamented that individuals with "serious mental illness" often "fall out of care" due to "transitions in health insurance."

MICHIGAN DEM SENATOR THROWS SUPPORT BEHIND CANDIDATE TO REPLACE HIM IN CONTENTIOUS PRIMARY

The couple reported nearly $686,000 in total income in 2025, underscoring the contrast between El-Sayed's calls for expanded government-backed healthcare and his wife's out-of-network psychiatry practice.

The couple reported $686,069 in total income and $675,246 in adjusted gross income on two pages of their 2025 tax return released Wednesday. El-Sayed also sports a collection of luxury watches ranging in value from $2,000 to $10,000 a piece.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS

"He regularly wears a SAR Rescue Timer on the campaign trail because he is trying to rescue our politics from corporate corruption," El-Sayed spokeswoman Roxie Richner told the Washington Free Beacon. "Sometimes he wears a vintage doctor's watch because he is a doctor."

Though El-Sayed earned a medical degree, he was never a licensed physician, which caused controversy amid allegations that he had claimed to be a practicing doctor.

"He has earned the right to be called ‘doctor’ twice over," a campaign spokesperson said at the time, alluding to the fact that he received both a medical degree and a doctorate degree in public health.

The El-Sayed campaign and Jukaku did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

item.title: JD Vance warns 'limousine socialists' will destroy Michigan auto jobs, depress American wages
item.description: JD Vance labels Abdul El-Sayed a "limousine socialist," claiming the Michigan Senate candidate's policies on immigration and tariffs hurt auto workers.
item.content:encoded:
Vice President JD Vance branded Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed a "limousine socialist," on Wednesday, warning that the far-left is using wealth redistribution and open-border immigration to undermine Michigan's working-class autoworkers.

Speaking on "The Ingraham Angle," Vance argued that the victory of Democratic candidates backed by the far-left exposes a party pushing wealth redistribution rather than domestic industrial growth.

"They're not promising you industry. They're not promising you good jobs. They're not promising self-sufficiency in a good industrial economy. What they're promising is redistribution," Vance told host Laura Ingraham.

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

The vice president addressed the primary victory of El-Sayed in Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate race. El-Sayed, a progressive backed by figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens and is now set to face Republican candidate Mike Rogers in November.

Vance said that primary victories for candidates further left of center reflect a broader shift in the party, arguing that the "base of the Democratic Party just wants radicals."

"It wants people who hate even the idea of private property ownership. But it also, I think, tells us that, that particular set of ideas is very popular in places you wouldn't expect because El-Sayed, he's this guy who holds himself out as a working-class hero, as a guy who's going to fight for the working class," Vance said.

"How does he fight for the working class? By flooding his state and his country with low-wage immigrants. Of course, those people will drive down the wages of the working class. And he also doesn't want to do anything to protect the Michigan auto industry. He has fought against the Trump tariffs that have saved the Michigan auto industry," he added.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Vance continued by labeling El-Sayed as one of the "limousine socialists" he said are anti-industry. While Stevens focused her campaign on manufacturing and the state’s auto industry, El-Sayed ran on a more progressive platform, advocating for "Medicare-for-All" and campaign finance reform.

"We've seen this in Europe and in the United States. The idea that you can build real prosperity by just redistributing assets from one group to another group. That's not how you build real prosperity. You have to actually sustain the foundation of the economy," Vance said.

"That is what the President of the United States has worked us towards for the past 18 months. It's going to continue to pay dividends," he added.

TOP WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST CANDIDATE CONFRONTED ON PAST 'DEFUND POLICE' RHETORIC

Watch the full interview with Vice President Vance on "The Ingraham Angle" at 7 p.m. ET.

item.title: MLB player Adley Rutschman's Red Sox trade ruined 'Spider-Man' movie plans with Orioles teammates
item.description: Adley Rutschman and three Orioles teammates were headed to see "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" when the MLB trade deadline call changed everything.
item.content:encoded:
The big-league movie plans were over before they ever began.

Adley Rutschman, Colton Cowser, Ryan Mountcastle and Gunnar Henderson had plans to see "Spider-Man: Brand New Day."

Then Rutschman's phone rang.

It was the Baltimore Orioles' front office with trade deadline news: Rutschman had been dealt.

MLB TRADE DEADLINE DELIVERS BLOCKBUSTER MOVES FOR ADLEY RUTSCHMAN FREDDY PERALTA AND KEVIN GAUSMAN

Among Monday's flurry of MLB headlines, Rutschman's move to the Boston Red Sox stood out as one of the biggest. The former No. 1 overall pick and three-time All-Star had spent his entire major league career in Baltimore.

Boston landed Rutschman and catcher Jake Rogers, sending top pitching prospects Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, outfielder Enddy Azocar, catcher Carlos Narvaez and a player to be named later to Baltimore.

A low-key afternoon with the boys quickly turned into an emotional goodbye for one of the Orioles' closest-knit groups. Speaking to the media a day later, Cowser described the ill-fated movie plans that turned into a trade deadline farewell.

"There was some shock there," Cowser recalled when describing the moment Rutschman received the news.

"You could kind of see it on his face that something might have been brewing up. I guess you could say there's a little bit of shock factor. It was pretty emotional yesterday. I think that the initial shock of it was something that was tough to see. Definitely some sadness there, and all I could do was give him a hug and tell him that I'm here for him and I love him. So yeah, it was obviously tough."

Cowser also reflected on what Rutschman meant to the clubhouse.

"He's an exceptional talent, can hit from both sides of the plate, exceptional on defense, and someone who's been anchoring this team for the past four-and-a-half years. He's truly going to be missed here. And as a friend, he's someone who's grown really close to me."

RED SOX FANS BEG TEAM TO TRADE 'TOXIC' JARREN DURAN AFTER YET ANOTHER EMBARRASSING INCIDENT

Rutschman, meanwhile, acknowledged the emotions of leaving the only organization he'd known while turning the page to Boston.

"Played my entire career there and been a lot of unbelievable memories, made a lot of great friends for life," Rutschman said, via MLB.com. "It's tough goodbyes, but we're onto the next thing and excited to be here and playing. It's all part of the game."

One minute, Rutschman was headed to see the friendly neighborhood web-slinger.

The next, he was headed to Boston, repping a brand-new team.

Over seven seasons, Rutschman helped transform the Orioles from a rebuilding club into an American League contender.

The 2022 AL Rookie of the Year runner-up developed into one of baseball's top catchers, earning three All-Star nods while batting .254 with 69 home runs, 277 RBIs and a .756 OPS (572 games) with Baltimore.

The Red Sox landed their catcher. Four Orioles never made it to the movies.

item.title: Trump's antitrust point man could reshape Big Tech cases against Google and Apple if confirmed
item.description: Adam Candeub's Senate confirmation hearing could reshape landmark antitrust cases against Google and Apple as he pushes for Section 230 reform.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's pick to lead the Justice Department's Antitrust Division testified before the Senate on Wednesday in a confirmation hearing that could shape the future direction of the government's fight against Big Tech.

If confirmed, Adam Candeub, a longtime telecommunications law scholar and former Federal Communications Commission general counsel, would take control of some of the most consequential antitrust cases in decades, including the Justice Department’s landmark lawsuits targeting Google’s dominance in online search and Apple’s control over the App Store and its rules for developers.

The cases could determine how aggressively the government pursues antitrust cases against the country's largest technology companies.

FOX NEWS POLL: MOVE OVER BIG BROTHER, VOTERS SEE BIG TECH AS GREATER THREAT TO US

As head of the Antitrust Division, Candeub would oversee those cases and decide whether to continue the Justice Department's aggressive antitrust efforts against the largest technology companies.

Candeub has emerged as one of the conservative movement’s most prominent critics of Big Tech, arguing that dominant online platforms have accumulated too much power and that regulators have historically overlooked the larger impact of technology companies on competition, speech and public discourse.

"Big Tech’s market power undermines our nation’s culture of vibrant democratic deliberation," Candeub testified before Congress in March 2023. "Elon Musk’s Twitter files demonstrated that Big Tech has indeed limited particular groups, including dissenters, from important government policies from full participation in national political discussions.

"This power to exclude threatens all Americans," Candeub continued. "Power to silence one group of Americans will be used sooner or later to silence another."

META MEDICARE SCAM ADS TARGETING SENIORS FACE SCRUTINY

Candeub has pushed for changes to Section 230, the federal law that protects online platforms from being held liable for much of the content posted by users. During Trump's first administration, he served at the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, where he helped lead efforts to narrow those legal protections for online platforms under Section 230.

And in his contribution to Project 2025, the conservative policy blueprint developed by the Heritage Foundation for a potential second Trump administration, Candeub argued that antitrust enforcement failed to account for the influence of major technology platforms over competition and the flow of information being shared.

"The large internet platforms have transformed the U.S. economy, streamlining consumer purchases, networking billions of people, and altering long-established business practices," Candeub wrote. "Despite their enormous size, they have avoided significant antitrust liability or prosecution. The reasons for this are not entirely clear."

Candeub’s nomination has drawn support from former Justice Department officials, including former Attorney General Bill Barr, who appointed Candeub as an associate deputy attorney general in 2020 during the first Trump administration.

TODD BLANCHE 'HONORED AND HUMBLED' BY TRUMP'S AG NOMINATION AFTER EXPLOSIVE WEEK OF FEDERAL ARRESTS

Barr praised Candeub’s expertise in telecommunications law and his academic background, describing him as a knowledgeable and capable leader for the Antitrust Division.

"I think he'll be a strong leader, and he's very knowledgeable," Barr told Fox News Digital. "I think he'll be balanced and fair and apply the law."

Barr is among more than a dozen current and former Justice Department officials who signed a letter to the Senate Judiciary Committee supporting Candeub’s nomination. The letter highlighted his experience at the FCC, the Office of the Associate Attorney General, the NTIA and his work as a law professor at Michigan State University.

INDIANA REPUBLICAN SENATOR MOVES TO BLOCK KIDS FROM ACCESSING PORN ONLINE

"Adam Candeub has the experience and the qualifications to live up to that storied legacy," the letter stated, arguing that the Antitrust Division’s next leader must be prepared to address the growing challenges posed by technology, social media and artificial intelligence.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"The Division’s next leader must be able to meet those questions with both intellectual seriousness and practical judgment," the letter continued. "Mr. Candeub is uniquely qualified to do so."

Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., said on X that he recently met with Candeub to discuss issues including merger reviews, Section 230 reform and efforts to protect children online.

item.title: Rita Wilson ignored her mother's old-school marriage advice, and it led her to Tom Hanks
item.description: Rita Wilson revealed on Michelle Obama's podcast the outdated marriage advice her mom gave before she found love with Tom Hanks on set in 1984.
item.content:encoded:
Rita Wilson is sharing the marriage advice her mom gave that didn't sit right with her.

During a recent appearance on Michelle Obama's podcast, "In My Opinion," the 69-year-old actress spoke about the outdated marriage advice her mom gave her before she met and married Tom Hanks.

"I was engaged before I got engaged to my husband. If I had married that person, I would have been divorced within a year," she said. "I thought that was what you were supposed to do at a certain age. I actually thought, because I had never really fallen in love with anyone, that I would be OK."

While engaged to that man, Wilson said she asked her mom for advice, telling her, "I don't know though. Should I marry him? I'm not really in love with him," and getting a surprising response in return.

'SHAMELESS' STAR EMMY ROSSUM REVEALS SECRET MARRIAGE AT 21 AFTER BOYFRIEND'S ALLEGED SHOCKING ULTIMATUM

"She said, 'Don't worry, you grow to love him.' I was like, 'Mom, that's not my generation,'" she said. "Her generation was like, 'Is he a good man? Will he provide?' There wasn't any of this, 'I have to be madly in love.' My parents were married for 59 years, so whatever they figured out, they figured out. But I still wanted to hold out for that falling in love thing."

Ultimately, Wilson did not go through with marrying the first man, knowing "marriage would not have sustained that relationship," and found love with Hanks after they reunited on set of "Volunteers" in 1984, tying the knot in 1988.

The "Now and Then" actress told Obama and her co-host and brother, Craig Robinson, when she "finally met Tom and fell in love with" Hanks, she had the feeling that "this is very, very different than what I had before."

When it comes to being a mom, Wilson said she wasn't sure she wanted to have children, but knew she "didn't wanna have children with the wrong people or person."

"Tom had two children," she said. "I already saw that he could be a good dad. So, I was like, 'OK, good, that's helpful. A little example here.'"

Hanks was already a father to Colin and Elizabeth, who he shares with his ex-wife, Samantha Lewes, and later welcomed sons Chet and Truman with Wilson.

Of his children, Colin and Chet have followed in Hanks and Wilson's footsteps, with Elizabeth pursuing a career as an author and journalist under the pen name E.A. Hanks and Truman focusing on other aspects of filmmaking.

Most recently, Chet has found success starring in "Running Point" alongside Kate Hudson, and Colin has appeared in a number of successful projects, including "Life In Pieces," "Fargo," "American Crime Story" and others.

"I’ve always asked him for advice when it comes to acting, and he’s always given me really great advice," Chet told Page Six in September 2024. 

"He just said, ‘If you just know your lines, and you show up on time, and you’re nice to everybody, that gets you a long way.'"

item.title: Viagra could do more than advertised as study reveals surprising health superpower
item.description: Sildenafil, Viagra's active ingredient, may restrict cancer metastasis by limiting cancer cells' cholesterol access, a new study has found.
item.content:encoded:
Viagra could do more than give men a boost in the bedroom, as new research suggests it may have benefits for cancer patients.

The prescription medication, which is manufactured and distributed by Viatris, is commonly used to treat erectile dysfunction by increasing blood flow during sexual stimulation.

It was originally developed to treat high blood pressure and chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart before researchers discovered its unexpected effect on erectile function during clinical trials.

PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS

A new study published by the American Association for Cancer Research found that the pill may have properties that can prevent cancer from spreading.

Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, led by Dr. Yarden Ariav in the lab of professor Ayelet Erez, found that Viagra’s active ingredient — sildenafil, a PDE5 inhibitor — may restrict cancer metastasis, or the formation of new tumors.

The team, which included scientists at the U.S. National Cancer Institute, analyzed human and mouse cancer cells, genetic experiments and 20 years of health data from 5 million members of Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest nonprofit healthcare provider and health insurer. They also examined how genes, proteins, fats, cholesterol and cellular energy interact.

The analysis revealed that sildenafil limits the cancer cell’s ability to make use of cholesterol, which is an important mechanism in how the cell breaks away from the primary tumor and migrates throughout the body, according to a press release from the American Committee for the Weizmann Institute of Science.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Sildenafil was found to block an enzyme called phosphodiesterase type 5, or PDE5, and increase the signaling molecule called cGMP, which dilates blood vessels – the feature that has made Viagra a successful treatment for erectile dysfunction.

According to the researchers, cGMP also binds to a protein that transports cholesterol within cells, reducing the cholesterol available for essential cellular functions. Cancer cells are "particularly vulnerable to this reduction in cholesterol supply," they noted.

Based on their findings, the researchers suggested that combining Viagra-related drugs with statins, which lower cholesterol, could help slow the spread of cancer by reducing tumor cells' access to both existing and newly produced cholesterol.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We have uncovered a new biological pathway that links a well-known signaling molecule to cholesterol regulation within cells and shown how this pathway can be harnessed to interfere with the ability of cancer cells to form metastases," Erez, senior researcher and dean of Weizmann’s Miriam and Aaron Gutwirth Medical School, commented in a statement.

"Beyond their therapeutic promise, our findings highlight that cancer biology is shaped not only by mutations in tumor cells, but also by the patient’s metabolic state and by medications they are already taking for other conditions."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The researcher added that this study "underscores the importance of treating the whole patient – not just the cancer – when tailoring the most effective therapy."

The study’s use of mouse models could pose a limitation to the final implications, as cancer treatment may not always translate similarly to humans, the researchers acknowledged.

The human evidence is also observational, which reveals an association instead of a proven cause and effect.

Fox News Digital reached out to the study authors and the medication's manufacturer for comment.

item.title: Fauci slapped with subpoena as COVID doc probed for 'profiting' off federal guidance
item.description: The subpoena seeks documents on Anthony Fauci's book deals, awards and alleged self-dealing tied to COVID-19 guidance that impacted Florida businesses.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A top Florida official is slapping Anthony Fauci with a subpoena over alleged "profiting" from federal guidance that hurt businesses, residents.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Wednesday he has issued an investigative subpoena against former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease Director Anthony Fauci.

The subpoena is part of a state probe into Fauci’s awards, incentives and guidance that impacted Florida’s residents and their businesses during the coronavirus pandemic.

FAUCI'S FIFTH FUELS VOW TO HAUL HIM INTO COURT 'EVERY DAY' DESPITE BIDEN PARDON

The announcement comes after Uthmeier, along with Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., pledged to have Fauci investigated at the state level following his Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee hearing last week when he pleaded the Fifth 111 times and references were made to his blanket federal pardon from former President Joe Biden.

"We issued a formal subpoena to Dr. Fauci under Florida state law, seeking a breadth of documents ranging to what he knew when he knew it, his doubts about the safety and efficacy of vaccines that he's out there promoting, and we're really focused in on his self-dealing," Uthmeier announced on Fox News.

"Evidence has come to light that he was trying to personally profit off of this. This is outside of his government duties, his official role: He's trying to pursue book deals, awards, get connected with high rollers that might help him come into millions and millions of dollars. This is wrong, and it could go towards a deceptive trade practice, fraud, public nuisance, you name it. I think there's many aspects of Florida law that now are implicated."

Uthmeier said the activities he is being subpoenaed over were revealed largely through his diary – several hundred pages of writings made on a federal server that Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., released last week.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"We know one award in particular, he made $900,000 on that," he said, appearing to refer to Fauci receiving approximately that amount from the Dan David Prize from Tel Aviv University.

Uthmeier said that when a bureaucrat is issuing directives and mandates he is privately questioning while also deriving a profit from that work, it raises legal questions.

"It starts as a civil inquiry," Uthmeier said. "But we're going to tie in all aspects of Florida common law, things ranging from deceptive trade, fraud, public nuisance, nothing is off the table."

The subpoena asks for awards Fauci applied to, considered or received from any organization, including those within the state of Florida, relating to the pandemic.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

It also asks for information on professional opportunities offered to or considered by Fauci, as well as interactions and communications with Florida businesses, media outlets and communities regarding COVID-19 vaccination sites, social distancing and mask orders, and school closures.

A pair of other states expressed encouragement at the news.

West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey alleged Fauci’s refusal to answer Paul’s questions is "concerning" and that the American people deserve to know whether they were misled or "manipulated."

"Both my Office and I support Attorney General Uthmeier’s efforts to uncover the truth," McCuskey said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill added that the public "deserves answers to about a million questions related to the pandemic, its origins, and the government’s actions in response."

Murrill alleged Fauci had lied and said that "we just don’t know how much" so.

"But he lied about something as basic as keeping a diary. The truth will come out."

Fox News Digital reached out to Schertler Law, counsel for Fauci, for comment.

Fox News Digital’s Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: Terrifying 'human safaris' on display in shocking video that reveals depths of Russia's deadly campaign
item.description: Video shows a Russian drone stalking a vegetable vendor through a Kherson market before detonating near him, in what Zelenskyy calls a "safari."
item.content:encoded:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of going "mad" following the release of a video showing a Ukrainian vegetable vendor being stalked by a Russian military drone before the drone exploded near him.

The incident occurred on Aug. 4 at a Kherson market located in Southern Ukraine. Footage released by the Kherson Regional Military Administration shows a drone hovering near a man standing beside a minibus before following him as he moves behind the bus. Moments later the drone dives toward the minibus and explodes near its front, detonating close to where the man is standing.

"A Russian drone deliberately hunted down a man selling vegetables and detonated right next to him," Zelenskyy wrote on X in a post including the video. "The Russians even admitted to the crime, showing zero regret and openly boasting about tormenting people. The man was wounded in the blast. Every single day, ordinary people in Kherson face these Russian "safaris."

MOSCOW BOMBING EXPOSES POTENTIAL SECURITY GAPS AROUND PUTIN'S MILITARY ELITE, EXPERT SAYS

The street vendor, identified as 52-year-old Yuriy, survived the near-fatal encounter, which Ukrainian authorities describe as part of a pattern of Russian drone attacks that track and target civilians — a practice they have dubbed "human safaris."

Speaking from a hospital bed, Yuriy told BBC that he and his wife were setting up their stall when he heard the drone buzzing nearby. His wife had run away, and the drone zeroed in on Yuriy, who pulled out vegetables to show that he did not have a weapon.

"It could see that I had tomatoes out, some cucumbers and eggplants laid out on the floor," Yuriy told BBC. "It even ducked under the umbrella when I was running away round the other side."

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the attack a "barbaric war crime," demanding international intervention.

WHY TRUMP IS DOWNPLAYING REPORTS RUSSIA AND CHINA ARE HELPING IRAN

Zelenskyy argued that everyone should see the video to make clear what Russia is capable of, arguing that President Vladimir Putin won't stop with Ukraine.

"This is not just about Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote. "Russia’s campaign against human life must be stopped here in Ukraine before it spreads further. item.title: Getting busted hooking up in a bar's bathroom is enough of a mood killer, you don't need to assault a manager
item.description: Hayley Serball allegedly spit on a manager's face after being confronted for having sexual intercourse in a bar bathroom in St. Petersburg, Florida.
item.content:encoded:
The mood is already ruined after you get busted hooking up in a bar's bathroom. There's no need to make matters worse for yourself, especially if there's any chance you can pick back up where you left off later on.

I think that's something most people can agree on. As a matter of fact, I assumed that was one of those unwritten rules everyone was aware of. You tried and failed to get away with a romantic encounter in a bar's bathroom.

It's unfortunate, but it does happen. But you move on. The whole night doesn’t have to be ruined because of it. If you're being escorted out of the bar and being sent on your way, take it. That's a sign all is not lost.

DITCHING HIS 'WHIZZINATOR' IN A PATROL CAR WAS FLORIDA MAN'S SECOND BAD DECISION OF DAY

That's a piece of advice that 19-year-old Hayley Serball could have evidently used last Saturday morning at a bar/restaurant in St. Petersburg, Florida. She allegedly had sex in the bathroom then spit on the manager.

Police say she was "confronted for having sexual intercourse in a bathroom" by employees of Shiso Crispy, reports The Smoking Gun.

As she was been escorted from the property, she allegedly turned around and spit on the manager, Kaleena Conklin's face.

It was noted by officers that "The spit was visible on the victim's face, and there were numerous witnesses of this."

I'd like to think there's a chance that she thought the move would restore the mood. I don’t know how or why, but I want to be as charitable as possible.

In any event, it didn't work. Serball was arrested on a misdemeanor battery charge and later released on $1,000 bond.

TSG reports that this isn't her first encounter with law enforcement and that she is currently a defendant in two pending felony cases.

One case stemmed from an auto burglary arrest and the other for an arrest for being an accessory after the fact to an aggravated assault with a firearm.

item.title: SEE IT: Michigan Dem predicts far-left El-Sayed will win Senate race after backing his primary rival
item.description: Sen. Gary Peters says Abdul El-Sayed will beat Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race despite backing Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., is confident that far-left Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed will defeat Republican nominee Mike Rogers in the race to replace him in the Senate, despite having endorsed El-Sayed’s primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens.

El-Sayed, known as a progressive insurgent, will go head-to-head with Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in the upcoming midterm elections. El-Sayed’s victory marks yet another win for the left-wing Democrats in this year’s primaries that have been battling to defeat the current Democratic establishment.

"I think if you look at the issues broadly, the differences between Abdul El-Sayed and Rogers when it comes to fighting for families in Michigan, it's pretty broad," Peters said to Fox News Digital when asked if his far-left positions could give Republicans a boost in Michigan.

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

He continued, "And in the end, that's why he will prevail."

Peters’ endorsement of Stevens over El-Sayed was part of a broader effort by mainstream Democrats to beat another progressive candidate, as Republicans largely viewed El-Sayed winning as a boost for their party’s chances to flip Michigan’s Senate seat. Rogers told Fox News Digital in an interview prior to the primary results that he would "beat either one of those candidates," but that El-Sayed has "his own special sauce of crazy."

The race between Stevens and El-Sayed was strenuous as it became a determining factor of whether Democrats could win the majority back in the Senate. More than $80 million was poured into this primary, qualifying it as the most expensive Democratic Senate nomination race in history.

DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE

Republicans have speculated that the turn to nominating Democratic socialist candidates indicates that the current Democratic establishment is losing its grip in these congressional races.

Peters pushed back on this claim, arguing that the results aren’t reflective of the entire party as this is "nothing new" for the state.

"Michigan is a very diverse state, and if you recall, Bernie Sanders beat Hillary Clinton many years ago in a primary in Michigan, so this is nothing new," Peters said, referring to the state's 2016 Democratic presidential primary. 

Sanders, I-Vt., endorsed El-Sayed in his Senate primary to defeat Stevens.

HASAN PIKER UNLOADS ON 'ISLAMOPHOBIC PIECES OF S---' DEMOCRATS AS EL-SAYED FACES PARTY UNITY TEST

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County Health Department director, would be the first Muslim senator. He has called for defunding the police and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He is also a strong critic of Israel, labeling the country’s actions as genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Peters declined to weigh in on where he falls on El-Sayed's policy positions — like defunding the police — despite expressing confidence the Democratic nominee will defeat Rogers.

"I'm not on the ballot, so I don't have to make those kinds of statements," Peters said.

El-Sayed and Rogers, who ran uncontested in his primary, will compete for the swing state’s Senate seat on Nov. 3 in midterm elections.

item.title: DoorDash gets FAA approval for its own delivery drones
item.description: DoorDash earned FAA Part 135 air carrier certification and launched DoorDash Air, but several operational approvals remain before drones reach customers.
item.content:encoded:
Your next DoorDash order could arrive with a flight path instead of a driver. DoorDash has earned FAA Part 135 air carrier certification and launched DoorDash Air, its in-house drone delivery program. The company now has federal authorization to operate a commercial drone delivery service in the United States.

Yes, the app you use for burgers, groceries and late-night snacks is entering the airline business. However, this does not mean a DoorDash drone will hover over your driveway tomorrow. The company still needs added operational approvals. It also has not announced its first markets or a firm launch schedule for its custom aircraft.

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?", has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE

DoorDash announced the FAA certification on July 29, 2026. The company says it is the eighth drone operator to earn this type of federal air carrier certificate. The FAA uses Part 135 certification for companies that carry other people's property for payment. For drones, it provides the regulatory path for commercial package deliveries beyond a pilot's direct line of sight.

Getting certified requires a five-phase FAA review. The agency evaluates the operator's aircraft, maintenance procedures and safety program. Even after earning the certificate, an operator still needs airspace authorization. It may also need exemptions or waivers for flights beyond visual line of sight. State rules and local land-use requirements can also affect where a delivery hub operates. So, DoorDash has cleared a major federal hurdle. Still, each real-world delivery network will require more planning and approval.

Anyone who has watched a hot meal slowly travel across town can understand the appeal. DoorDash says more than 20% of its orders in 2025 traveled between three and five miles. Those orders took nearly 25% longer than shorter trips, according to the company.

DoorDash blames part of that delay on the challenge of matching a Dasher with a mid-range order. A driver may prefer several shorter deliveries near a busy restaurant area instead of one longer trip. A drone could take the longer order while a Dasher remains close to restaurants. As a result, the customer could get a faster delivery while the driver moves on to another nearby order.

DoorDash estimates that drone deliveries completed during 2025 took an average of about 25 minutes. The company also says some locations in its partner drone pilots saw order volume rise by roughly 30%. That increase continued during the nine weeks after the pilot began. Those are DoorDash's figures, so performance could change by location, weather and the type of order. Still, they help explain why the company wants more control over the aircraft carrying its deliveries.

CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'

That is the same robotics and autonomy group behind DoorDash's Dot delivery robot.

DoorDash says its drone will be designed and built in the United States. The majority of its components will also come from the U.S., according to the company. DoorDash has not revealed the aircraft's range, payload capacity or final design. A DoorDash spokesperson told CyberGuy that the company plans to share more details about those specifics this fall.

DoorDash says Dashers will continue handling the vast majority of its daily deliveries. That makes sense. A drone cannot walk into an apartment building or carry a large catering order upstairs. It also may struggle with bad weather or a location without a suitable drop zone.

Instead, DoorDash wants its Autonomous Delivery Platform to select the best method for each order. The platform can assign a Dasher. It can also choose an autonomous option such as Dot or a drone.

For example, a small order traveling four miles to a suburban house may fit a drone. A large grocery order going to a high-rise apartment will likely need a person. This approach follows a broader shift across the delivery industry. Uber Eats has also moved toward drone deliveries, while other companies continue testing robots and airborne delivery systems.

FAA certification gives DoorDash the legal foundation to operate an air carrier. It does not provide blanket permission to begin unlimited drone flights in every city. DoorDash has not announced its first DoorDash Air markets. The company also has not provided a detailed timeline for deliveries using its in-house aircraft.

In addition, longer autonomous routes may require FAA approval for beyond visual line of sight operations. Local zoning, environmental reviews and community concerns can also shape where hubs are built. Noise could become a major issue. The FAA notes that drone noise may bother a community even when it falls below the level of a significant environmental impact.

Therefore, early service will likely remain limited to carefully selected areas. Suburban neighborhoods with predictable routes and open drop-off spaces may prove easier than dense urban blocks.

JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA

DoorDash drone delivery could shorten the wait for small, urgent orders. Cold medicine could arrive without waiting for a driver to cross town. A nurse finishing a long shift might get a hot meal faster. A forgotten phone charger could reach you before your battery runs out. However, availability will depend heavily on where you live. Your address may need to fall within an eligible drone delivery zone. The order must also meet the aircraft's weight and size limits. DoorDash told CyberGuy that it is testing the aircraft to operate across a wider range of weather conditions and climates. The company said it will pause operations during extreme weather until conditions return to an operable level.

You should also look closely at the final cost. DoorDash has not said whether its new in-house DoorDash Air service will carry a separate fee or change how tipping works. The company also has not explained whether customers will choose between a DoorDash Air drone and a Dasher once the new service launches. DoorDash's current partner-operated program does allow eligible customers to select drone delivery at checkout.

For now, think of DoorDash Air as an important step toward wider service rather than a nationwide launch. The federal certificate gives DoorDash the regulatory foundation to operate its own commercial drone delivery service. However, individual operations may still require airspace authorization and other FAA approvals. The next test will be whether DoorDash can make drone delivery reliable enough for an ordinary Tuesday night dinner. For more background on how companies are already testing airborne orders, check out how drones are changing food delivery.

DoorDash has spent years learning how to move orders through streets. Now it wants to control what happens in the sky. FAA certification gives DoorDash Air a serious start. The company has the app, the restaurant relationships and billions of past orders to study. It also knows where deliveries slow down. Still, building a drone is only one piece of the job. DoorDash must prove that its aircraft can operate safely and consistently. It must also keep food intact while avoiding noise problems and neighborhood resistance. Human Dashers are not disappearing. Instead, DoorDash wants drones and robots to handle specific trips that could be faster without a car.

It's been a quiet summer for Natalie — probably for the best — but she returned to social media this week to debut a new partnership with Jedora Jewelry.

And as you know in NASCAR, sponsorship is everything:

"Barbie has a great day every day. Ken only has a great day if Barbie looks at him. A little sneak peek into what’s coming @jedorajewelry."

No real clue what that means or why Natalie is showing off some red lingerie under firesuit to promote a jewelry line, but it's good to have her back in the swing of things after a tough season.

For those wondering, Decker has three O'Reilly Series starts this season with finishes of 33, 33 and 34. Credit for the consistency, I reckon.

OK, let's leave the track and move this party over to the diamond, where Houston Astros outfielder Taylor Trammell had one of tougher moments of the entire MLB season earlier this week.

Not really sure how you come back from this:

Just a brutal look for Taylor Trammell. Humiliating. Devastating. I can't even imagine what's going through his head when he touches home and then realizes what he just did.

How do you look your teammates in the eyes after that jog? Goodness. Better yet, how do they look him in the eyes after?

Do they laugh? Do they try to pick him up? Do they just ignore it and act like it never happened? I think you almost have to laugh. I would.

I'm a big believer in laughing through the pain, and this feels like the only way through this scene. Lordy.

The good news? Taylor buckled down, went back to the drawing board, and actually hit one over the wall last night!

All's well that ends well! Good for Taylor Trammell. The Baseball Gods never disappoint.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Hump Day class into a Hump Day night. I've got a yard to mow before it rains for the 27th straight day down here in Florida.

First up? Let's go from one embarrassing moment to another:

I mean, it's just perfect. Everything about that clip is perfect.

The blind dart throw to the rim. The mebound. The put-back. The yelling and shouting and screaming, all while losing by 20.

It's just perfect. Is Angel Reese a content machine, or what? I can't get enough of her. Between the play on the court, and the absolute nonsense off of it — including her comments before Monday's "Barbie Game Day," which celebrated Reese's signature Barbie doll — I'm all in.

What comments, you ask? Oh, you know, just when she told the media that was so proud of her Angel Reese Barbie doll because she didn't grow up with Barbie's that looked like her.

Black Barbie dolls, by the way, have been around since the Carter Administration. Angel was born in 2002.

Moving on ...

Waiting all day for a Sunday night!

Yes, Amber got Carrie yesterday, but whatever. We respect Carrie Underwood around here. There is no greater feeling than the one you get on a Sunday night in the fall when the SNF anthem comes on after your team won earlier in the day.

It's euphoric. It gives you chills every time. For us old enough to remember, it also came with a little dread, because it signaled that school was about 12 hours away and you hadn't done an ounce of homework over the weekend.

But still, you got chills when it came on.

Welcome back, Carrie. Welcome back, football.

And welcome back, "Hard Knocks" ... apparently:

Remember back in the day when "Hard Knocks" was appointment viewing? It was the unofficial start of the fall. The first "Hard Knocks" intro of the year, with some sort of pep talk from the coach followed by the iconic theme, was the true "Wow, football is really back" moment.

Now? Hand up, I had NO idea it was on last night. None. Zero. I didn't even know the Seahawks were the featured team this year.

What a fall from grace.

That being said, I'll watch it tonight. And then probably forget about it.

But man, what a theme.

See you tomorrow.

Did you know "Hard Knocks" was on last night? Email me at Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

item.title: 'We thought we would die': Passengers thrown into ceiling during terrifying flight
item.description: Thirteen flight passengers and four crew members were hospitalized after severe turbulence struck an Air India plane, triggering an aviation investigation.
item.content:encoded:
Seventeen people were injured after an Air India flight experienced severe turbulence, sending passengers into the ceiling and aisle during a sudden loss of altitude.

The flight — traveling from Phuket, Thailand, to New Delhi, on Tuesday, August 4 — experienced what the airline described as a "sudden loss of altitude" while cruising. The aircraft continued flying normally and landed safely in Delhi, an Air India spokesperson said in a statement posted on X.

The flight was carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members. Thirteen passengers and four crew members were injured and taken to hospitals for medical evaluation, the airline said.

SHOCKING MID-FLIGHT BRAWL ERUPTS AFTER TAKEOFF, SENDING FLIGHT BACK TO AIRPORT

Five passengers were discharged as of Monday evening, while the remaining injured passengers and crew members continued receiving treatment, the airline added.

"Air India’s foremost priority remains the safety and well-being of its passengers and crew. We will continue to support those affected and their families and will work closely with the relevant authorities throughout the course of the investigation," the airline said in its statement.

The aircraft briefly lost about 300 feet in altitude during the turbulence, The Times of India reported.

Fox News Digital reached out to Air India for further comment.

"It's very unusual but not rare to have serious turbulence incidents," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From the Wing," told Fox News Digital in an interview.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"For there to be an injury of some kind in turbulence is about one in 1.2 million departures."

Leff advised travelers to always take precautions. "You should still wear your seatbelt when you're seated on the plane," he said.

"Four of the six flight attendants on board this flight were hurt," he added. "They're up in the aisles, they're working, they don't have the opportunity most of the time to stay belted. It is more dangerous."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Passengers on the flight described terrifying moments inside the cabin as people were thrown from their seats and into the ceiling.

"It was a traumatic experience. My father was sitting next to me, and when this happened, his head touched the ceiling," Palak Raniwala, the daughter of one of the injured passengers, told news agency ANI. "It was a terrifying experience for all of us."

Raniwala said the turbulence was unlike anything her family had experienced before and recalled hearing panic in the voices of the crew.

"The flight attendants were panicking, and the pilot himself seemed rattled — you could hear the nervousness in his voice," she told ANI. "The whole situation left us terrified."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Another passenger, identified as Viviana, told the outlet that the flight appeared to be operating normally before the turbulence suddenly struck.

"The aircraft seemed to be moving normally, but suddenly the turbulence began," she told ANI. "I saw my sister thrown into the air from her seat. My mother was knocked on the head."

"We thought we would die. It was really scary. I was shaking and crying," Viviana added.

He added, "Flying is still a lot safer than driving. If you drive, you shouldn't be concerned with flying."

item.title: Nuclear experts urge Trump not to let Iran steer talks away from regime's atomic threat
item.description: Nuclear experts urged President Trump to keep Iran’s nuclear program at the center of talks, warning Tehran could seek sanctions relief before addressing remaining nuclear capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
Iran’s top Revolutionary Guard commander declared Wednesday that Tehran would continue working on nuclear weapons as long as the United States and Israel possess them, intensifying concerns that Iran is using negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz to postpone concessions on its nuclear program.

"As long as the United States and Israel possess nuclear weapons, we will continue working on them for our national security," IRGC commander-in-chief Ahmad Vahidi said, according to a translation of remarks circulating Wednesday. "If they disarm, we will disarm."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded by vowing that Israel would continue preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, with or without a diplomatic agreement.

WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY

"Today, we heard the commander of the Revolutionary Guards, Vahidi, explicitly declare Iran’s intention to continue developing nuclear weapons — ‘continue,’ as he put it," Netanyahu said at a ceremony marking the reinterment of Shimon and Rivka Herzl, the grandparents of the founder of modern day Zionism, Theodor Herzl.

"Well, as prime minister of Israel, I too am determined to continue — to continue preventing Iran from possessing nuclear weapons," he said.

Netanyahu praised President Donald Trump as Israel’s greatest friend in the White House and expressed appreciation for the two countries’ joint efforts against Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

"Israel’s existence is not subject to negotiation," Netanyahu said. "With an agreement or without an agreement, I am determined — we are all determined — to do whatever is necessary to ensure our security and our future."

NETANYAHU'S ISRAEL GRAPPLES WITH TRUMP-IRAN DEAL AS DETAILS REMAIN UNCLEAR

The exchange came as nuclear experts urged Trump to keep Iran’s nuclear program at the center of negotiations, warning that Tehran could use the Hormuz crisis to secure sanctions relief and other concessions before addressing its remaining nuclear capabilities.

Trump told "Fox News at Night" Tuesday that military force remained an option if Iran abandoned the talks, while insisting Tehran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.

"If they back out again, they’re going to get hit really hard," Trump told Fox News’ Trace Gallagher. "They know that. They understand that. I have no choice. They can’t have a nuclear weapon. It’s very simple.

"The hard hit is yet to come, and hopefully we won’t have to use it."

Trump said negotiators held an "all-day negotiation" Tuesday and described the discussions as "very good." He has said the talks would initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz before turning to Tehran’s nuclear program.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN

Andrea Stricker, deputy director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Nonproliferation and Biodefense Program, said that sequence could play directly into Iran’s strategy.

"It is in the Iranians’ interest to steer the negotiations toward the issues that they most care about," Stricker told Fox News Digital, including securing major U.S. concessions over Hormuz and "maintaining control of that crucial waterway that has proven a lifeline for Tehran to survive this war."

She said Iran would also seek oil sanctions relief and potentially relief from all U.S. sanctions, before addressing the nuclear file.

"If Tehran is able to structure the talks that way — and I’m concerned that Trump appears to be going along with that approach — there may be little left in terms of leverage to get big concessions from the Iranians on the nuclear file down the line," Stricker said.

There is evidence that Tehran has sought to sequence the talks in its favor. Axios reported in April that Iran proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war before beginning nuclear negotiations, potentially reducing U.S. leverage over enrichment and Iran’s enriched-uranium stockpile.

The Washington Post later reported that Tehran was focused on preserving its leverage over Hormuz rather than engaging deeply on major nuclear restrictions.

Kelsey Davenport, director for nonproliferation policy at the Arms Control Association, agreed Iran is seeking to capitalize on the leverage it gained by disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

"The current focus on the Straits of Hormuz is not surprising. Iran is looking to capitalize on leverage gained by disrupting maritime traffic through the waterway and test if Trump is willing to negotiate in good faith," Davenport told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

She said Tehran understands that any durable agreement will ultimately have to address its nuclear program but said, "At the end of this conflict, Iran will still possess the capabilities necessary to build a bomb," Davenport said, "The relevant knowledge and nuclear expertise cannot be bombed away.

"Tehran retains key materials and technologies necessary to build a bomb," she added. "If left unchecked, the nuclear program will be a source of instability and renewed conflict, even if Iran does not resume more proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities."

A proposed agreement between Iran and Oman could give Tehran some control over ships entering the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters Wednesday. One regional source described the arrangement as a concession that had already been made, although the precise meaning of Iranian "control" remained under negotiation.

Iran is also seeking fees from ships traveling through the waterway, according to Reuters, while Washington has opposed both Iranian control and mandatory transit charges.

Stricker said postponing the nuclear issues would allow the regime to preserve its remaining enriched-uranium stockpiles and avoid fully dismantling its nuclear infrastructure.

She said Iran also wants to avoid accounting for its past nuclear weapons-related work or committing to end uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing.

"Leaving them as a last-order issue in the negotiations likely means that we will not see the Iranians make big concessions and make a solid nuclear deal," Stricker said.

Davenport said the administration should prioritize restoring access for inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency before beginning detailed nuclear negotiations.

"The IAEA has not visited key Iranian nuclear sites in more than a year," she said. "It remains unclear how much of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure remains and where any gaps might be in trying to account for Iran’s nuclear materials."

She said renewed inspections would give Washington a clearer picture of Iran’s remaining facilities and materials, while helping negotiators design a verification regime capable of addressing any gaps.

Davenport also recommended pairing sanctions relief with specific, verifiable Iranian steps rather than negotiating one sweeping package.

"A series of smaller deals could build confidence in the process," she said.

Stricker urged the administration to link every concession involving Hormuz, sanctions or the U.S. blockade to a measurable Iranian step on the nuclear file.

"The best approach to ensure a solid deal is to make the nuclear issues just as important as the Strait of Hormuz, removing the blockade and other top Iranian priorities," she said.

item.title: LEE CARTER: Election shocker: The winners had a slogan; the losers just had résumés
item.description: Political candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Wesley Bell and Trump's 2016 playbook reveal why Tuesday's primary winners had a sentence, and the losers had a résumé to read.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday night, the left won. The right won. The establishment won. The insurgents won.

In other words, nobody won.

Except for the message.

100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE

The political class will now perform its traditional postmortem: Find the result it agrees with and declare a sweeping ideological mandate.

But voters delivered a simpler verdict: Tell me what you are going to do for me, and please do it before I lose interest.

The real divide was not left versus right. It was memorable versus forgettable.

'SQUAD' MEMBER'S COMEBACK BID THWARTED AS ESTABLISHMENT DEMS NOTCH VICTORY AGAINST SOCIALISTS

The winners had a sentence. The losers had a résumé.

Consider Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary.

His message was "Money out of politics. Money in your pocket. Medicare for All."

Eleven words. Three beats. A villain, a benefit and a policy. In that order.

DAVID MARCUS: IN BOOMING DETROIT, VOTERS SKEPTICAL OF SOCIALISM SNAKE OIL

Politicians like to imagine voters carefully comparing policy frameworks. Voters are usually wondering why everything costs so much and whether anyone in public life has noticed.

Stevens made the respectable case: experience, credentials and electability. All of that may have been true. It was also about her.

"I can win" is not a promise to voters. It is a candidate asking the public to participate in her career planning.

A résumé is evidence. It is not a reason. No one has ever left a rally humming, "She performs well in hypothetical general election matchups."

DEM PRIMARY ERUPTS AS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE DISMISSES RIVAL AS ‘CELEBRITY CANDIDATE’

The same dynamic appeared in Missouri, although ideology changed costumes.

Former "Squad" member Cori Bush warned that billionaires and outside interests were trying to control her district.

Her opponent, Wesley Bell, answered with six words: "Progressives are supposed to make progress."

It was a lethal little sentence.

EX-'SQUAD' MEMBER FIGHTS FOR COMEBACK AS SOCIALIST WING RAMPS UP WAR ON DEM ESTABLISHMENT

Bell took a word Bush believed she owned — "progressive" — and handed it back with a new definition: not posture, purity or national attention, but results.

Bush offered an enemy. Bell offered a standard.

A villain alone is not enough. It is only the first half of the argument.

The complete version is: They are doing this to you, and I will do this for you.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

Too many candidates never reach the second clause. They mistake indignation for persuasion.

But anger is an accelerant, not a destination. It can start the car. It cannot tell you where you are going.

Donald Trump understood this in 2016.

China was taking the jobs; he would bring them back.

Washington had lost control of the border; he would build the wall.

America had been diminished; he would make it great again.

Villain. Action. Benefit.

FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS

One could object to every detail and still understand the whole thing before the elevator doors closed.

Republicans saw their own version in Michigan’s gubernatorial primary. John James spoke about restoration, work, security and a Michigan comeback. Perry Johnson emphasized a sweeping audit of state government.

An audit may be useful. But it is a process.

A comeback is a promise.

Politicians adore process words because they sound responsible. Voters hear paperwork.

They are not dreaming of an interagency working group. They would like the electric bill to go down.

This may be why data centers became one of the night’s more revealing issues.

William Lawrence made opposition to unchecked data center development central to his Michigan campaign. He took something vast and abstract — artificial intelligence infrastructure — and brought it home.

"AI infrastructure policy" is remote.

"Your family may pay more to power someone else’s data center" can move votes.

The closer an issue gets to the kitchen table, the less ideological it feels.

That is also why affordability has become the great unifying language of recent elections.

Politicians with little else in common have discovered that voters are preoccupied with the same rude facts: rent, groceries, child care, healthcare and the shrinking distance between a paycheck and a minor financial emergency.

But "affordability" is not, by itself, a message. It becomes persuasive only when people can picture it: the prescription they can fill, the rent increase they avoid, the utility bill they can manage.

Voters do not experience the economy as a set of indicators. They experience it as a series of small humiliations.

The grocery cart edited at checkout. The dinner out quietly canceled. The home that now seems permanently one promotion away. The medicine postponed.

The party that speaks most clearly to that experience will have an advantage. The one that answers with macroeconomic data will deserve what happens next.

Tuesday’s results also suggest something we should not miss.

Americans can be anti-establishment and anti-mayhem at the same time.

They can want change and reassurance. A fighter and a grown-up. Someone who will break the right things and leave the rest of the house standing.

This confuses political professionals, who prefer voters to fit neatly into ideological boxes.

Voters persist in being people.

The quality that matters is not always moderation. It is translation.

Can a candidate turn an ideology into an outcome? A policy into a picture? A political argument into something people can see in their own lives?

Tuesday’s winners were not uniformly progressive, moderate, populist or establishment.

What they shared was the ability to place the voter inside the story.

Too many political appeals begin with "I."

I fought. I led. I delivered. I have a plan.

The voter is expected to applaud this autobiographical achievement and infer a benefit.

The stronger appeal begins with an understood "you."

Your money. Your town. Your family. Your future.

Every campaign should have to pass a second-person test.

Can voters hear themselves in it? Can they explain what changes if the candidate wins? Can they repeat the central idea in 10 seconds?

If not, the campaign does not have a message.

It has material.

Both parties will now produce impressive documents announcing that voters endorsed whatever the authors believed on Monday.

But voters may have said something less ideological and more useful: Stop making us work so hard.

Do not hand us a list and call it a vision.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Do not describe your ambition and call it our future.

Do not give us a villain and forget the rescue.

Tell us what is wrong. Tell us what you will do. Tell us how life will be different.

Then stop talking before you ruin it.

Tuesday night was not a triumph of the left or the right.

It was a triumph of the personal over the procedural, the promise over the résumé and the memorable over the merely correct.

The winners gave voters a sentence.

The losers gave them something to read.

item.title: WNBA silent on whether French transgender star dominating women's league would be eligible to play
item.description: Julie Tétart led France's LF2 in scoring and rebounding, but the WNBA and WNBPA won't say if the transgender player is eligible under the CBA.
item.content:encoded:
The WNBA and the Women’s National Basketball Players Association still have not said whether the most dominant player in a French women’s professional basketball league would be eligible to play in the WNBA.

Transgender basketball player Julie Tétart, a biological male, plays for Monaco in Ligue Féminine 2 (LF2), France’s second-tier women’s basketball league.

Tétart averaged 21 points and 20 rebounds per game during the 2025-26 season, leading LF2 in both categories.

FRENCH TRANS PHENOM JULIE TÉTART LOOKS WNBA-READY — SO WHY HASN’T THE ‘INCLUSIVE’ LEAGUE CALLED?

Eurobasket.com also named the 34-year-old its All-French LF2 Player of the Year, Defensive Player of the Year and Domestic Player of the Year.

Those numbers certainly sound WNBA-worthy.

Plus, Tétart told OutKick/Fox News Digital that playing in the WNBA is "a childhood dream" and said, "If they contact me, I won’t say no."

So, OutKick/Fox News Digital asked the WNBA and the Women’s National Basketball Players Association a simple question: Would Julie Tétart be eligible to play in the league?

Neither organization responded to the initial inquiries or a subsequent follow-up specifically addressing Tétart’s eligibility under the collective bargaining agreement.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT TO PROTECT GIRLS AS WNBA ALL-STAR INITIATIVE BACKS ‘GENDER-EXPANSIVE’ GROUP

The question shouldn’t be difficult. After all, the league’s newly signed CBA appears to provide a clear eligibility standard.

Article XIII, Section 1(a) states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."

Sounds simple, right?

But as OutKick/Fox News Digital previously reported, the 409-page agreement never defines "woman" or "women." The terms "transgender" and "gender identity" don’t appear anywhere in the document.

The CBA contains detailed definitions for dozens of other terms. Yet the agreement doesn’t define the word that determines who may play in the league.

That omission was already notable when Indiana Fever star Caitlin Clark said leagues and governing bodies should work with athletes to determine who should be included in women’s sports.

OutKick/Fox News Digital previously sought clarification about the standard after Clark’s comments.

At that point, the league could treat the question as theoretical.

It isn’t theoretical anymore.

Tétart gives the WNBA a concrete case: a professional player in a women’s league who led LF2 in scoring and rebounding and has publicly expressed interest in the WNBA.

Would the WNBA consider Tétart a "woman" for purposes of Article XIII?

Would eligibility be determined by biological sex, gender identity, hormone levels or some other standard?

CHERYL REEVE SENDS CLEAR MESSAGE TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM WITH ‘TRANS KIDS BELONG’ SHIRT DURING FEVER-LYNX GAME

The CBA doesn’t say, leaving the league’s eligibility standard unclear.

The question is separate from age, draft and international-player eligibility provisions, which the CBA addresses in detail.

The WNBA has repeatedly presented itself as an inclusive, progressive sports league. But "inclusion" doesn’t answer the basic question: What is a woman, according to the WNBA and the WNBPA?

Either Tétart is eligible or Tétart isn’t.

If Tétart is eligible, the league should explain the standard and how that standard protects fairness for female players.

If Tétart isn’t eligible, the league should identify the rule or policy that makes a biological male ineligible. The CBA’s current language doesn’t provide that clarity publicly.

This isn’t a request for the WNBA to comment on an abstract political debate. It’s a request for the league to apply its own eligibility rule to a specific professional basketball player.

The same applies to the WNBPA. The union agreed to language stating that only women may play in the league, so players deserve to know how that language would apply to a biological male currently dominating a women’s league.

A professional player has publicly expressed interest in a WNBA opportunity.

The league has a rule that supposedly determines whether that opportunity is possible.

But when asked whether Julie Tétart qualifies under that rule, the WNBA and WNBPA had nothing to say.

item.title: Senate confirms new CDC director as diarrhea-causing parasite outbreak sweeps US
item.description: Dr. Erica Schwartz was confirmed as CDC director along party lines amid concerns over whether she would stand up to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on vaccines.
item.content:encoded:
The Senate confirmed the next director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as viral outbreaks wreak havoc across the country, and as lawmakers worry whether they’ve found someone to stand up to President Donald Trump’s top health official.

The upper chamber confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz to be the next CDC director on Wednesday along party lines. Her confirmation comes as a Cyclospora outbreak, commonly known as the diarrhea parasite, carves its way across the U.S. from contaminated lettuce.

Schwartz is the latest person to lead the agency during Trump’s second term in a position that has seen nearly a half dozen different names and faces helming the nation’s disease-fighting outfit.

CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW

She almost didn’t make the cut for a full confirmation vote.

Lawmakers on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee grilled Schwartz on whether she would actually stand up to the Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his position on vaccines.

Notably, HELP Committee Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., who proved the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy last year, didn’t buy whether she would just take orders or make scientific and medically-based decisions.

TRUMP BLASTS SEN BILL CASSIDY AS ‘DISLOYAL DISASTER,’ PUSHES CHALLENGER JULIA LETLOW IN LOUISIANA GOP PRIMARY

When pressed during her initial committee hearing whether she would buck orders that were politically motivated, Schwartz told Cassidy, "The secretary will absolutely allow me to be CDC director."

"I feel like I’m having to go after this question a little bit more firmly than I feel like I should," Cassidy said. "You can be CDC director and just take orders. We need a CDC director that will actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization."

That changed, though, and Schwartz cleared her committee test. Cassidy, who has used his newfound freedom to test the waters against the administration after being ousted by a Trump-backed opponent in his primary, said the agency "needs someone who understands that the way to prevent vaccine-preventable diseases is to reassure the public that vaccines are safe and effective."

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK SPARKS BACKLASH, SPLITS MAHA MOVEMENT

"I’m confident that she knows what she is doing and will stand against those who do not," he said.

Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, is not the first CDC director to be confirmed during this Congress.

The first was Susan Monarez, who lasted only a month in the role.

Monarez received glowing praise from Trump during her confirmation process, but was swiftly booted from the position over what appeared to be a disagreement with Kennedy over vaccines.

item.title: Commanders filling wide receiver need with Stefon Diggs, leaving Brandon Aiyuk to stew in his odd behavior
item.description: The Commanders chose Stefon Diggs over Brandon Aiyuk, whose off-putting behavior has NFL teams privately expressing concerns about his locker room fit.
item.content:encoded:
The Washington Commanders, desperately wanting to add wide receiver help for their offense, had basically two obvious and productive veteran options from which to pick – Stefon Diggs or Brandon Aiyuk.

So, the guy who has played for three different teams the past three seasons and somehow wore out his welcome despite producing two 1,000-yard seasons in that time – Diggs?

Or the guy who signed a big contract with the San Francisco 49ers in 2024, got injured, didn't play in 2025, and has become a candidate for an intervention because of his bizarre behavior in recent months – Aiyuk?

STEFON DIGGS FOUND NOT GUILTY ON STRANGULATION AND ASSAULT CHARGES, NOW EYES NFL FREE AGENCY

The Commanders are going with Diggs.

Diggs is set to sign with the Commanders, NFL Network first reported on Wednesday. Diggs will agree to what is expected to be a one-year contract and it will not be a minimum salary deal.

Diggs will join a wide receiver room replete with other veterans, including Terry McLaurin, Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffery and Dyami Brown, all who must produce while rookie Antonio Williams develops.

This is good for Diggs.

He's from the DMV (D.C., Maryland, and Virginia), he's coming off his first fully healthy offseason in three years, and he's once again playing with a good quarterback in Jayden Daniels.

This is not good, however, for Aiyuk.

It's a full-on public statement of what NFL personnel people have been privately telling Fox News Digital about Aiyuk's behavior. It is filled with off-putting, perhaps even disconcerting antics, and teams don't want to add that to their locker room.

What antics, you ask?

BRANDON AIYUK'S SOCIAL MEDIA POST MOCKING KYLE SHANAHAN'S CAR CRASH DRAWS BACKLASH AND COULD COST HIM A JOB

There's more but you get the drift.

Aiyuk didn't hide his desire to go to the Commanders because he desperately wants out of San Francisco and Daniels was his college teammate at Arizona State, where the two had good chemistry.

The Commanders expressed some interest in Aiyuk with the 49ers months ago.

But that interested waned. And now one can only imagine how Aiyuk will react to the news that the team offering his best chance for playing this season is going in another direction.

It might serve as a lesson for him to cut back on his reputation-harming conduct.

Or not.
